en.title: Invitations and abilities
en.goal: Invite someone to do something, say what you know how to do or can do, and make polite requests.

lessons.saber-conseguir: Saying what you know how to do or can do

vocab: to want / to be thinking of doing something
to know how to (a learned skill)
can, to be able to (ability/permission in a situation)

phrases.t: I want to go see a movie.

dialogue.title: Invitation to the movies
lines: I want to go see a movie. Can you come?
At 7 in the evening, at the movie theater.
Sounds good, I want to see that movie too!

hui-vs-neng.title: "Huì" or "néng"?
hui-vs-neng.body: Huì (会) is a learned skill — something you know how to do because you learned it. Néng (能) is ability or permission in a specific situation — it depends on your schedule or circumstances, not on skill. English uses "can" for both, but Chinese keeps them apart.

xiang-vs-yao.title: "Xiǎng" or "yào"?
xiang-vs-yao.body: 想 (xiǎng) expresses a softer wish to do something — closer to "would like to" or "I'm thinking of". 要 (which you saw in Unit 5) sounds more direct, like "I want", especially for requests.
examples: I want to go see a movie (softer)
I want a cup of tea (direct request)

qing-please.title: 请 (qǐng) — polite requests
qing-please.body: 请 (qǐng) is like "please" when it comes before a request or invitation — a simple, polite way to soften a direct instruction.

dou-all.title: 都 (dōu) — "all"
dou-all.body: 都 (dōu) means "all" or "both", but it always comes right before the verb (after the subject).

ye-also.title: 也 (yě) — "also"
ye-also.body: 也 (yě) means "also" or "too", and just like 都, it always comes before the verb, not at the end of the sentence the way "too" often does in English.
